## Load libraries and read in data to utilize in this week's class

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false

## Load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(maps)
library(mapdata)
library(mapproj)
library(fishualize)
library(praise)
```

```{r}
## Read in data
# Population in California by county
popdata <- read_csv(here("Week_07", "Data", "CApopdata.csv"))

# Seastar counts at field sites in California
stars <- read_csv(here("Week_07", "Data", "stars.csv"))

# View data
view(popdata)
view(stars)
```

## Practice with pulling map polygon boundaries and creating a map
```{r}
# Pull map polygon boundaries for the world
world <- map_data("world")

# Make a map of the world
ggplot()+
  geom_polygon(data = world,
               aes(x = long, y = lat,
                   group = group,
                   fill = region),
               color = "black") +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  theme(panel.background =
          element_rect(fill = "lightblue")) +
  coord_map(projection = "mercator",
            xlim = c(-180,180))

# Yay, I made a map!
praise()
```
## Practice making a state map

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: fig-CA-map

## Filter states dataset to California
states <- map_data("state")
CA_data <- states |>
  filter(region == "california")
view(CA_data)

## Make a map of California
ggplot()+
  geom_polygon(data = CA_data,
               aes(x = long, y = lat,
                   group = group),
               color="black")+
  coord_map()+
  theme_void()
```
@fig-CA-map shows a simple map of California. Next, we are going to add some data onto the map.

## Practice adding data onto a map
In this section, we are adding county population data to our map. First, we need to pull county data and check the population data. 
```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false

## Pull county polygon data for California
counties <- map_data("county")
head(counties)[1:3,]
head(popdata)
```
Next, we need to make the column names of the county and population data match in order to join them.
```{r}
## Create dataframe with population and county data in California using renaming and joining
CApop_county <- popdata |>
  select("subregion" = County, Population) |>   # Rename columns to match counties
  inner_join(counties) |>
  filter(region == "california")                # Make sure it reads only counties from California, since some county names repeat in other states
head(CApop_county)
```
Now that we have our joined data of population and counties within California, we will make a map of California with the dataframe we just created. 
```{r}
## Create a map of California with population by county
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = CApop_county,
               aes(x = long, y = lat,
                   group = group,
                   fill = Population),
               color = "black") +
  coord_map() +
  theme_void() +
  scale_fill_gradient(transform = "log10")   # Use log10 to compress the color scale so less-populated counties are still visible alongside Los Angeles

## What a fun map!
praise()
```
Next, we are going to take this map we just created and layer points of seastar data on top.
```{r}
## Look at seastar dataset
head(stars)

## Use same map from the previous step and add sea star data
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = CApop_county,
               aes(x = long, y = lat,
                   group = group,
                   fill = Population),
               color = "black") +
  geom_point(data = stars,
             aes(x = long,
                 y = lat,
                 size = star_no)) +
  coord_map() +
  theme_void() +
  scale_fill_gradient(transform = "log10") +
  labs(size = "# stars/m2")

## Save the map
ggsave(here("Week_07","Outputs","CApop.pdf"))
```
The seastar dataset shows seastar counts (per m2) at field sites in Califonia. 

Now that we have learned how to create basic maps using the maps package, we will learn about the sf and rnaturalearth packages!

```{r}
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(rnaturalearthdata)

## Call in world map in sf
world_sf <- ne_countries(scale = "medium",
                         returnclass = "sf")
## Make a map in sf
ggplot(world_sf) +
  geom_sf(fill = "lightgray",
          color = "white") +
  coord_sf(crs = "+proj=robin") +
  theme_void()
```
Pau with learning about how to make basic maps!
